utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it you can follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Anna Richterova, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin? And I see new faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm John Ackerman and I'm here with David Cunningham and our new case manager/legal assistant, Mr. Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and welcome, Mr. Vujic. You come at a crucial time in this trial when we are approaching the beginning of the case for the Defence and both Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Cunningham will need your help immensely. So I count on your cooperation. Yes. Any preliminaries? No. We have some. Mr. Ackerman, I know you have had problems and I know that you still have problems. I am just reminding you that we are expecting still from the Defence your response to 92 bis motions filed by the Prosecution with regard to Bosanska Krupa, a motion filed on the 8th of April; Sipovo, a motion filed on the 8th of May; Kotor Varos, a motion filed on the 6th of June; and Bosanski Novi, a motion filed on the 28th of November of last year. Now, this one we had already handed down a decision regarding one witness statement. I think we decided that on the 17th of January but you can check. And then there was disclosure to you of statements regarding other witness -- another witness, sometime in February or March of this year and you can check on that. We would like you to, if possible, file your response on all these by the beginning of next week so that you enable us and the Prosecution to proceed without any major problems, because obviously if there are objections which we uphold then obviously the Prosecution would have to bring over the witnesses, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I'll do the best I can. The issue with regard to Sipovo, that was not filed because the witness was apparently not coming and without a viva voce witness, then there can't be a Rule 92 bis witness if the issue is cumulative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least we need to know. I am -- I and my colleagues, my two judges, we are never informed of these things unless you tell us, you or the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I still don't know if there is going to be a witness from Sipovo. The schedule indicates the possibility of that and I think that's the best the Prosecution has right now is the possibility of that so I suppose it makes sense that in honour of that possibility, I should go ahead and try to file that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours must understand that the body of work to be done between now and the end of the Prosecution's case exceeds our ability to do it. So there are parts of it that are simply not going to get done. I can't tell you what's going to have to drop off the edge, but something is going to have to because we are just not physically capable of doing all the work that has to be done by the middle of August. We have now been reduced to two weeks to file our brief. It's not possible, can't be done so you're going to get something less than what ought to be filed and that's going to be the way it is from now on, as near as I can tell, until we get to the middle of August. And I regret that. I regret it terribly. I wish my health was better so that I could do a better job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think there are options, Mr. Ackerman. I'll discuss it with my colleagues but I don't think there are options.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't understand why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Especially when you consider that our Rules consider that seven days is enough for a 98 bis brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We gave you double.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think if you look at the history of the Tribunal, that no Defence has ever been given less than 30 days and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For 98 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, it's significantly more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, you're wrong. You're wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And significantly more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're wrong. You're way wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know I mean it's -- I concede that I may be but I know that in, especially in the more difficult cases, that that time has exceeded 30 days in a number of cases and this is the most difficult case ever tried here yet and to reduce that time and we started out we had a month and then yesterday, because apparently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had a month because -- I mean, you had a month and you didn't have a month. You had a month because it happened to coincide with August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what we had, I'm looking at the schedule, what we had was from the end of the Prosecutor's case until September 5th, our motion was due on September 5th and now all of a sudden it's due on August 15th which takes away three weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank Ms. Korner for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why should I be punished for what she did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not punishing you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm feeling pretty punished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not punishing you. I mean, basically, as it is you would have worked the whole of August, now you only have to work half of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that is not a gift. And actually I shouldn't say you're punishing me, you're punishing Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not punishing Mr. Brdjanin either. We think that 15 days, 14 days, for preparing the Rule 98 is enough. If you convince us that it is not enough, we are open on that and we can try and review it. But that would mean still that you would have to work in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've already resigned myself to that, Your Honour. I told you this in our meeting the other day, that I'd given up on that issue. I probably should file a formal motion instead of talking about this with you in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you ought to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's probably the thing for me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you ought to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've noticed that Mr. Sebire is here. No one informed me that he was coming back this morning. Fortunately, I did bring my materials and I will go ahead and proceed with my cross but it would have been nice to have had at least 20 minutes' notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My last words yesterday to the Prosecution was that if -- to liaise with you if Mr. Sebire was going to come over this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That didn't occur, Your Honour when he walked in the courtroom this morning it was a total surprise to me but I can go forward, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can cut the other problem short. Would three weeks be enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd hesitate to ever say that any amount of time is enough but it is better than two, Your Honour. I'd prefer to file at the end of August. That would be my preference. The original schedule, the one that we were handed in your chambers, showed my motion due on September 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you also -- that was taking account of the court recess as being a court recess, particularly since you had shown a desire to be able to rest as well in August. And by allowing a whole month for the filing of the Rule 98 bis motion, we were taking that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think -- just, Your Honour, if I were to file on September 5th, as has been set out originally, it doesn't change anything with regard to the balance of the plan with regard to concluding this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course it does, Mr. Ackerman. Of course it does. We are working an extra week when we were not scheduled to work and that's in July. And that changes everything. Moves everything by one week forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I understand that. I'm just talking about the end game, that if I were to file on September 5th as planned in this original schedule that you handed out to us that changes nothing with regard to the balance of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I also told you in the meeting that we had that this is a desperate attempt to conclude by the end of August. And it allows for no space at all in case we have a calamity, no space at all, and that is my problem. So each time I can find even one day which I can gain, I will go for it. Anyway, I would suggest you file a motion and we'll see exactly what has happened in other cases. I have a report actually on all the other cases that have been here on 98 bis, and what was recommended to me originally, that we would give you two weeks and that would be more than enough compared with other cases. But if you're not happy with that, I think we can move to three weeks without any difficulty. Mr. Sebire, welcome back. Usher, please -- yes, go ahead with the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think Ms. Sutherland or Madam Richterova at least an apology in public to Mr. Ackerman is due if no one informed him that Mr. Sebire was coming this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I apologise but it was our understanding that because Mr. Ackerman wasn't feeling well yesterday that it was postponed to today so I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed, Mr. Ackerman. Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sebire.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think as we broke the other day we were talking about that paragraph on page 4 of your report of 28 August, 2002, which was S281-E in the Stakic case and I had gone through that paragraph dealing with the purpose of the report and what you said in there about the purpose of the report, and it talks, among other things, about the different approach that the Bosnian authorities had from that of the OTP forensic people. The question that I want to ask you next about that is this: If the Bosnian authorities were undertaking these exhumations and even welcoming observers and cooperation from the OTP as was the case, for instance, at Jakarina Kosa why was it the OTP found it necessary to independently conduct exhumations and go to the expense of putting together teams to do that? Why was that felt necessary?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cooperation which was provided to the Bosnian authorities in the case of some exhumations took place after the forensic programme of the OTP had already ended, that is we did not have a full team -- full teams on the site to conduct all the exhumations and post-mortems of the individuals in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, are you saying that these exhumations would not have been done but for the OTP putting together a team to do them?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not quite what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the exhumations would have been done in any event by the Bosnian authorities and my question is why the OTP felt it necessary to become involved in this process beyond simply in an observer and assistant status to the Bosnian authorities. That's what I'm trying to find out.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you conduct investigations, when you collect information about a crime, if the victims of that crime have not been discovered, then it is quite normal to try to find them, to find their bodies, where they were buried, and the OTP tried as much as possible to take care of the exhumations, that is, the disinterment of the bodies and up to the forensic analysis. It was later that it was decided if we were -- did not integrally conduct this because they were not capable of doing all that and therefore we sought to seek assistance in forensic -- in the forensic work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is it your position that that to some extent, the work done by the Bosnians was deficient, certainly in the forensic realm and the OTP felt that needed to be enhanced to some degree?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not what I'm trying to say. I do not think that what I'm saying is being misinterpreted. You're quoting the example of Jakarina Kosa and this is a very interesting example because the day when the exhumations were finished, there were 330 bags with body remains were taken out of that site. At that time, the number of -- from the documents that were found there, it was clear since I was there, that we were faced with a place where there were victims coming from different places, that is, from different places within the municipality of Prijedor and that it had happened at different times. So in order to identify them we had to conduct -- it was important for us to conduct the forensic examination at that time and we had two forensic pathologists from Bihac but we needed to expedite the whole process of the forensic examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like you to in that same report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They want you to slow down. Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sebire, the interpreters from the French or English booth have asked me to draw your attention if possible you could slow down the speed at which you are answering the questions. Thanks. Mr. Ackerman, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention now to page 10 of the same report, the Stakic report. Underneath the first table on that page, the following language appears: "It should be mentioned that in April and May of 2002, an OTP monitoring team conducted excavations with the assistance of the Bosnian authorities in the area of the Tomasica mines and the Benkovac barracks. Several locations were excavated within both areas and did not reveal evidence of any individual or mass graves. Hugh Tuller, archeologist, is currently preparing the reports detailing these operations." Now, as I understand it you basically went out in those areas, the Tomasica mines and the Benkovac barracks and dug holes looking for bodies. And failed to find any. True?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it that you had some information that caused to you believe that you would find bodies there?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that information came from? What was that information?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was information that was obtained either from witnesses or by other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As regards witnesses, in other words, what you're saying is people who claimed to know told you that you would find individual or mass graves at these locations and directed you to the specific area where you should conduct your excavation? Correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons claimed in one hand that there were mass graves on a site and that we should check, but we thought that there was a probability that -- but we have not found any one or anything in places which were not indicated with utmost precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Also, what you said in answer to my first question about where this information came from, either from witnesses or by other means. What other means?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mostly the information which proceeds from Article 70 of the Statute of the Tribunal, as said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that information apparently turned out to be incorrect also?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, because we found nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 43 of that same report, sir, and this is a section of the report where you're setting out in some detail links between parts of the Stakic indictment and the results of exhumations and in this particular section you're talking about the allegation in the Stakic indictment about the killing of a number of men in Trnopolje camp between 28 May and October of 1992, and what you said in that report was that as of that day, the date of that report, no links between exhumations and crimes committed in Trnopolje camp have been established. Does that remain the case today?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to talk now about some information contained in the addendum of 16 May, 2003, that is Exhibit P2008. And I want to refer you to page 9. And the information I'm referring to here is found throughout, I think, in various places in all three of the reports but you talk about the ethnicity of persons exhumed and there is one person you refer to of another nationality but I couldn't find in any of the reports that you had identified that nationality. Can you tell us what it was?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't mention the precise nationality of the person who had been exhumed, in that the exhumations were on going and you couldn't exclude the possibility of discovering people in these grave sites of other nationality. In this case, it has connection with the municipality of Kljuc and if I'm not mistaken, the exhumation that took place at Laniste 1, this person was of German nationality, who remained in the village of Biljani and died around the 10th of July, I think, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: He comes from the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean? Who comes from the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said -- this person or the remains were of a person of German Nationality who remained in the village of Biljani and died on the 10th of July, I think in 1992. And then the interpreter came forward with saying he comes from the Second World War. Who came from the Second World War, Mr. Sebire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, to be more clear, according to information I was provided with about this person, it was a German soldier who remained in ex-Yugoslavia after the Second World War and lived in this village, lived there until the 10th of July, 1992. I apologise for not being clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That makes sense now, thank you, Mr. Sebire, thank you the interpreter for highlighting the matter. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm glad you did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was a little mystery there, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to Jakarina Kosa I want to talk to you about that. You were present throughout virtually all of that exhumation process, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what was the role that you played there? What specifically did you do?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noted all elements that were discovered in the course of the exhumation, the number of bodies and body parts. I did this on a daily basis. The exhibits, the evidence that was found such as gas masks, plastic cans, explosives, or what appeared to be explosives later on. The names that we could discover on the papers that were found there. This was done in order to have a daily record of everything that had been discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, a lot of things were found in addition to bodies and skeletons and things of that nature. You found, as you just mentioned, identity papers; right?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Certain identity papers were found, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You found watches and jewellery of various forms?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, I would like you to look at some exhibits and look at each one and then put it on the ELMO so we can all see it and describe what it shows, if you will. Now, these come from -- Your Honour and Prosecution, from P2010 and the ERN numbers of each of the photographs of course appear on them and I'll ask the usher to give them to you. When you've looked at the first one and you're satisfied you can talk about it, then put it on the ELMO for us, would you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Put them on the ELMO, please and then we can try and follow up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This one is 02130100; is that correct? Is that the number that shows in the upper right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what we see there is a gas mask?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's basically resting where it was found at Jakarina Kosa; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at the next photograph, then. This one is from P2010, its number is 02130298. What do we see there?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It looks like military unexpended ammunition, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this photograph, this is ammunition that wasn't used in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Let's look then at the third photograph, again from P2010, and it's 02120968, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 02129968. And what we see in that photograph is a soldier's helmet; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You can bring those photographs back now. I believe, Your Honour, these photographs are all part of the record. I think they are contained on one of the CD's that's P2010 that's already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. I think it is like that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to speak to you now just very briefly about the exhumation at Redak and you were involved also in that excavation, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And again, during that excavation, other than bodies and skeletons, other items were found such as watches and jewellery and identity papers; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. As well as ammunition. In this case, they were used cartridges, rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Several expended rounds there; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the forensic report said that there were a minimum of 300, about 300 gunshot wounds to the bodies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to go now back to your testimony from the 30th of May, page 16733.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While Mr. Ackerman is looking into the document, is Witness BT56 informed that his testimony is being delayed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe that you're talking generally, sir, about the exhumation process here. And you're talking about the -- how one determined the ethnicity of persons who are exhumed. You gave this answer on page 16732, line 24: "As far as the ethnicity of the victims is concerned, the main source of information was obviously the identification of the victim." And then there is some more of that answer that apparently didn't make it into the transcript. Judge Agius then asked the analysis points to which direction? This is the answer I'm interested in, sir: "With regard to all the bodies that were exhumed for which we tried to determine the ethnicity, 1300 were Muslims from Bosnia, 10 were Bosnian Croats, 3 were Serbs from Bosnia and in one case, the person was of another nationality, a nationality that differed from the three previous ones mentioned. And in other cases we weren't able to determine the ethnicity, we didn't have enough information that would allow us to determine the ethnicity. In 55 cases, we didn't have such information." Just briefly, you certainly cannot determine nationality by looking at the skeleton of a person, can you, in the instance of these cases?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't determine the nationality of the person just by looking at the skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So one way you could determine nationality is if there was clothing associated with the body and in that clothing were identity papers? That was -- that would be a way?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be an indication. Finding papers on a person, does not necessarily mean that this person, the person mentioned on the papers, is the person, is the actual body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's true, not necessarily. If there were clothing on the body that was very distinctive like a hand-knitted sweater that a relative could identify as having been worn by that person when last seen, that could be useful in determining identification; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, it would be an indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For instance I noticed with regard to the exhumations done at the Vrhpolje Bridge that there were numerous photographs of very distinctive sweaters, very distinctive designs that appeared in the data base from that exhumation and I assume their purpose was to try to promote identification of persons who were found there.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since you're going back to the exhumation at Vrhpolje Bridge, I'd like to remind you that with regard to this exhumation, I wasn't present for part of it, and for the other part, I consulted documents that I received about this exhumation. In addition to the fact that the Bosnian authorities proceeded to identify the bodies, 12 on one side of the bridge, 13 on the other, some of the bodies had been identified on the 3rd of June, 1992 in the course of the investigation conducted by --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sebire, I'm not interested in all that or I would have asked you. The only thing I asked you was I assume that the numerous photographs from that exhumation of distinctive clothing with distinctive designs were there to try to promote identification of the persons found there. That's all I'm asking you, nothing more. And I think you can say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in fact that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. The same page of your testimony, down in line 19, you say this, about identification of ethnicity, "In the case -- in cases in which an unidentified individual in a grave site was exhumed, at a site where other members of that ethnicity were exhumed, in such cases, that individual would be taken to belong to the same ethnic group." Correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in such cases, but if we have a clear indication at the same time that there were no attempts to change the state of the exhumation site.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your report in the Stakic case, and again that's Stakic Exhibit S281-E, page 5, you say roughly the same thing: "In some instances, the ethnicity was determined even though the victims were not identified. The main reason being that these unidentified bodies were exhumed from graves where other bodies identified as Bosnian Muslims were recovered." Correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be correct to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you said, "It is more likely that the large majority of the 760 bodies for which the ethnicity was not determined are of Bosnian Muslim ethnicity."

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, it's correct, isn't it, that with regard to these ethnicity determinations, based upon the basis we have been talking about, you're engaging in a presumption, aren't you? You're presuming that if A is true, then B follows?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If in the course of an exhumation at a particular site here, you find a certain number, a number X of bodies, and you've identified them, and you've identified the number of victims in this site corresponds to information on the number of people who died in this incident and in addition the site has no traces of the -- having been attempts to change the site, none of the bodies were moved, since they were buried there. In such cases, one does assume that it's more likely that these people are other victims from the same incident than from other incidents. And that is the reason for which I have said that it is likely that these people belonged to the same ethnicity, without affirming this of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, but my question remains and I'd like you to answer it: You're engaging in a presumption, the presumption being that if A is then B follows? And I think you can tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's explained it clear enough, Mr. Ackerman. And the Chamber can draw its own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so the numbers of Muslims that you are listing as having been discovered, a number of non-Serbs that you're listing as having been discovered in these various exhumations, that number is actually enhanced by this presumption that you engage in regarding if A is true then B follows; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring -- if you have a look at the last report that I made you'll see on the last page that it has to do with the people identified a given number with reference to date of the report, if I can go to this page, it's the 16th of May, 2003, you'll see that the unidentified bodies were excluded from the final number, from the total number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the presumption doesn't even come into play with regard to the total number of 1872, is that what you're saying to us?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of the 1872, a certain number were identified. The 588 were -- remaining bodies were taken from the sites and they were linked to the incidents on the basis of testimony and other evidence. Page 12, you can see that these 584 bodies that have not been -- unidentified, it's an approximate number because in certain cases, some bodies were identified, others were exhumed, so we provided a number and we wanted to exclude the problem that you have mentioned, the problem that you have raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Another issue now. I was reading the transcript of your testimony in the Stakic case and I ran across a part of it that causes me to ask you the question. There was some discussion, in fact there was a question from Judge Schomburg, about it, about a list of missing persons maintained by the Red Cross and I take it you're familiar with that list?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't established by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I have to read you what appears at page 8866 of the Stakic transcript, a question by Judge Schomburg, because now with your answer, I'm totally confused. Judge Schomburg said to you, and I think dealing with a list of alleged victims that came from Bosnian authorities, I'm not certain. I can look if you don't remember. But anyhow, Judge Schomburg asked you this: "Did you compare this list of missing persons with the last update of the Red Cross list of missing persons?" And your answer was, "No, I received that list only recently. I saw it only recently. And therefore I had no time to either compare it or go through that." Now, I conclude from that that there is a Red Cross list of missing persons that you had recently received when you testified in Stakic. Am I correct or not?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately that's not what is at stake. The list that I received was a list that had been updated on persons who were missing in the municipality of Prijedor. Earlier on I was referring to a list that was published in April of 2002 by this same association that referred to the list of missing people and when I was testifying we had just received a new list in an electronic form which we couldn't read and it caused many problems at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what is the Red Cross list of missing persons that Judge Schomburg is talking about?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the International Red Cross has lists of missing persons for Bosnia and for many other countries. The question that was put to me was whether I had compared the new list received from the association that listed missing people in the municipality of Prijedor with the list of missing people that the Red Cross

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a question, now that you've had a lot more time, have you done that? At the time you said you hadn't had time to do it. Have you been able to do it since the -- I guess the 6th of September?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that date, if I'm not wrong, I produced tables listing all people who had been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's an answer. What you told Judge Schomburg was that you hadn't made a comparison with the Red Cross list because you hadn't had time and that was the 6th of September. I'm wondering in the several months since then, if you have had time to make that comparison.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with regard to the 3.200 individuals that are listed, the 3.200 missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's now go back to the addendum that you filed with regard to this case, P2008, 16 May, 2003. Under, "Considerations," you talk about the various aspects that were taken into consideration with regard to each of these persons. It's page 6 of the report. It's 7894, the last four numbers of the ERN number. You talk about the ethnicity of the victims, the status of those exhumed at the time of their death, the cause of death of the persons exhumed and the time and location of the death. What I'm interested in talking to you about now is the status of those exhumed at the time of their death. When you speak of status, I take it what you're speaking of is whether the person was military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very precisely, when at the time of death a person was a combatant or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of the things that you indicate under B, status, is clothing recovered in the course of the exhumation. In that regard, does that mean that if they are not found wearing a uniform or in the presence of a uniform, you concluder that they're non-combatants?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Quite the contrary, the discovery of military clothing could perhaps tell us that persons perhaps were combatants at some point in time, as I have said it was an indication. One needs more than just the clothing to come to a conclusion, but that is an indication, that is not the only element that is taken into account. As you can see, there is also other testimonies of witnesses or the next of kin of the victims, if the victims have been identified, who can provide us with information about the status of that person at the time of that person's death. So that helps us to establish whether a person at the time of death was a civilian or a person who was a combatant but who was then arrested and subsequently executed or was it a person who died in the course of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what role does clothing recovered in the course of the exhumation play?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say that in the first -- at first, it helps to -- towards the identification of a person, but in addition to clothing, there are all the other elements which are found near a victim, such as the wallet or shoes or things which belonged, which are specific to an individual and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you conclude from the presence or absence of military uniform that someone either was a combatant or not a combatant?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not only on the basis of that. You have to take into consideration --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Everything just stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I thought you interrupted me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, not at all, okay. Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question that you were answering, would you conclude from the presence or absence of military uniform that someone either was a combatant or not a combatant and then you started answering that question. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was saying was, if you exhume a body, an individual who only has a skeleton and you have no other information concerning -- allowing to identify that person and you cannot draw any conclusions until the time of identification through other procedures which are more scientific, such as DNA analysis. At an exhumation site where you have a large number of bodies, for instance, we can take Redak, which you already mentioned sometime ago, all the bodies could not be identified. Some skeletons had the remains of clothes, and some bodies which were not identified were related to incidents which happened in July of 1992, at the football pitch in Ljubija and then along the mining road from Ljubija to Stari Majdan, that was another place of incident. The number of victims at the exhumation site we did not see any attempts to alter the -- to alter the site, and there were these skeletons without any clothing or any other identification elements but it is nevertheless highly likely, if not positive, that these persons were victims of those incidents and elsewhere you can also receive the testimony of the survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there are a couple of things in that answer that I want to ask you about. One of the things that you mentioned was that clothing wasn't enough. You sometimes would get DNA analysis. How does DNA analysis help you decide whether someone was a combatant or a non-combatant?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The DNA analysis makes it easier to identify somebody on the basis of this identification, you try to communicate either with members of families or witnesses who can provide you with information with regard to the circumstances under which that person died, and it's the basis of this information which is collected that we tried to establish what happened to that particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But these would be the same kinds of witnesses who told you to go dig up Benkovac barracks and you'd find bodies there? This is not necessarily reliable information, is it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you are slightly wrong there, when you speak about a member of a family who saw somebody who had been taken out by the police or the army or had been exited. I don't think that such a person can make such a mistake. If you have information from a person who says, "I believe that a particular place you have a mass grave," then that is another matter and then the investigation allows to you either corroborate or not the information received. The fact that we go to a place as you have mentioned which is Benkovac or Tomasica for instance, where indeed we did not find anything but it doesn't mean that there is nothing there, we are simply saying that there was nothing at the place which we were told about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me just be clear of my concern, sir. If what we were doing here was dealing in an exploration to try to come up with our best guess about what we can tell, that's one thing. But you must understand that what's going on here is a criminal trial, where there is a presumption of innocence and where it's the burden of the Prosecution to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt and my concern is that you are engaging in a number of presumptions with regard to your testimony that are presumptions in favour of the Prosecution and against the defendant rather than the other way around. It would seem to me that if you're going to make a presumption, that the presumption would have to be that the person is a combatant unless you could prove beyond a reasonable doubt otherwise. But you're presuming just the opposite, it seems to me. Am I wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I just said, there are elements which allow you to draw certain conclusions, at a moment when one is capable of identifying the bodies and when you have the testimony of witnesses, then it is very difficult to -- unless you have the testimony, then it's very difficult to speak with such certainty as you are as spiring to and if you look at the general comment at the end of my report, you once again can see that we excluded bodies which were not identified. From 58 sites of graves, 13 further individuals were exhumed and all these related to 30 incidents which are mentioned either in the indictment or which were mentioned by witnesses in their testimonies before this Court. So I would not say that these were simply presumptions. I think that would be going too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in many cases, what you're giving us is your best guess based upon the information available and that's a far cry from proof beyond a reasonable doubt, it seems to me, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is how you understand it, unfortunately I cannot say anything more on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go to another subject now and talk about how you establish date of death. To some extent you used the same kind of methodology when you made determinations about when it was that the people found in these graves were killed, and I'm looking now at -- it's your progress report dated 13 August, 2001, Exhibit P2007 and I'm on page -- the ERN number is 02090497. And again, you engage in what you call a logical conclusion or which might be a presumption again, that if you're able to -- if you're able to prove by independent sources that -- you're still paging around. I better wait until you find your spot. The ERN number at the top right-hand corner of the page is 02090497. It's section 2.6 of that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he's found it, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you're engaging pretty much the same kind of exercise there, if you find persons in a grave that you can establish were killed say in July of 1992, what you're saying is it's then logical to conclude that everyone else you find in there was killed at about that same time. And you're saying that that would -- you'd also have to establish the grave site had not been disturbed to draw that conclusion; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the other problem, of course, that you don't talk about there, which you have in fact encountered is that the bodies put in a particular grave site don't necessarily all come from the same place. For instance a grave site might be a place where bodies are taken from several locations and re-interred and therefore you couldn't make the conclusion that you talk about as being logical, could you?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You are quite right. You already mentioned the example of Jakarina Kosa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Unless you actually know the date of the burial, it's quite difficult to estimate a date of death after the passage of a number of years, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, as for the date -- for establishing the time of death, it is the first thing you need is the identification of the victim and the tracing of the last moments. This is basic importance to establish where that person -- when the person -- when the person died. So, for instance, if we take this Jakarina Kosa, the information that we received on the site was pointing towards the summer of 1993, and then the evidence that we collected in the meantime showed us that those were actually persons who died in 1992, that these persons who died at different times in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are running at a tangents here. First of all, Mr. Sebire, your terms of reference in the task that you had over there, did it include also establishing the time of the death of these persons or was that left in the hands of other forensic experts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment -- when a person is identified, that is my task, to go through the evidence which has been collected meanwhile by the OTP if we can find any information regarding the death or the disappearance of a person. In some forensic reports, there was a probable delay, that is, it could have been because there was a delay from the time. They could have been done five or six years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question. Were you in charge also of establishing the date of the interment, of the death, or was that exercise left in the hands of someone else, some other forensic expert? That's my first part of the question. And then I come to Mr. Ackerman's question. Were you in charge only of the exhumation stage and the preservation of the evidence or were you also tasked to then carry all the analysis, scientific and otherwise, to establish the identification and also the date of the death and possible interment of that person, those persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the date of death or disappearance of the exhumed person, yes, indeed, that is an integral part of my work, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And the part of the question that is highly relevant coming from Mr. Ackerman is this: Short of or in the absence of direct and specific information as to the exact date of death of the persons that have been identified, is there a scientific test that you can resort to in order to establish the date of the death based only on the remains and the surroundings in which those remains are? Or do you have to base yourself on circumstantial evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond briefly, I'm an investigator, I'm not a scientist, I'm not an anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you. Why was -- why were you tasked with doing all this when you're not a scientist and you're just an investigator? Who was supposed to establish the death of a person, based on the remains found in a grave or the -- the forensic expert, the forensic scientist or the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It all depends on the bodies which are found. A forensic pathologist can give you a period, for instance, a body was found in the year 2000 and then perhaps on the basis of tests that are conducted, one can say that they have been there for ten or 15 years, on the basis of various information. When a post-mortem are conducted we attempt the identification. In this the role of investigator is of course to act on the information received, to try -- about the person, to find the next of kin and all the rest that has to do with that particular individual. As for role of the forensic pathologist, he can give us the cause of death and on the basis of that, we can try to find witnesses and establish the circumstances under which that person died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sebire. I give him back to you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you're saying, sir, is this: If you find somebody in a grave, who you're able to identify, as a certain human being with a name, and you're able to establish by some independent source, either by a relative or an eyewitness that that person disappeared on July 4th of 1992 and was never seen again, that you conclude then that that person must have met their death in 1992 and based upon that conclusion, you then say to us it's logical to conclude to the other persons buried in the same grave died around the same time. I mean that's basically what you're telling us, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. That is not what I said. If you go back to what I said previously, I made a certain nuance and said what I was saying -- because I tried to give you more explanation as to the time when one could really make very serious assumption that bodies found at the same site. At the time we could not do it, so I cannot really answer yes or no to your question because I need to give you a much more nuanced answer and I do not know whether I should now go into this explanation or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm trying my best to rely on what you have written in your various reports and we had referred, sir, to that report entitled, "Progress report dated 13 August, 2001," Exhibit P2007, and what I read and I'm going to read it again, that you said was this: "In these cases," and you make an exclusion here, "When the exhumation does not indicate that the grave site has been disturbed," then you say this, "It is logical to conclude that the unidentified individuals have been killed at the approximately same time as those identified." And I conclude from that, if you're able to identify someone from a grave or someones from a grave having been killed at a certain time, then you presumed that everyone else in there was killed at the same time. Isn't that what you're saying? And if I'm wrong, please tell me how I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will allow myself to go back to the exhumations at Redak, if that will help answer your question better, and if you allow me that perhaps will be the most telling example. In the case of that exhumation, we found 63 bodies that -- a limited number of bodies that were found at the site were identified. They all -- it all comes on from -- on the basis of the information from survivors of the same incidents where these people fell victim and they gave us an approximate number of the victims of that incident. The information given us by those witnesses, that is the gunning down of these people and that would for instance, correspond to the information that we were provided by the pathologists. Then we take the -- then if you look at what was found on the skeletons, that is the wounds that were found on the skeletons and it showed that there were four or five bullet shots per person, and we found some 300 bullets, projectiles in the bodies. At the same time, we -- and there was nothing that we found that that site was disturbed after those bodies were put there. So we base our conclusions on the integral body of information that we receive collected -- either collected from the site itself or the testimonies and if all that tallies, then it is logical to conclude that all the persons found in that mass grave were victims of one and the same incident and naturally, not all the bodies from that same site were identified, when we were able to communicate with members of family and witnesses to -- in order to verify whether they knew the names of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And that's -- you've described Redak, which is not a typical exhumation. That analysis you just gave us doesn't work at all for Jakarina Kosa. It doesn't work at all for Hrastova Glavica, for example, does it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Jakarina Kosa, yes it was much more complicated because we had victims who -- of different incidents and different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Hrastova Glavica, two of the bodies found there were from the Second World War; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the documentation that we received, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, how much more time do you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It looks, Your Honour, like a half hour, a little bit less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll break now, then, if it's convenient for to you break now, and we will resume in 25 minutes from now. That's 5 to 11.00. And Ms. Sutherland, I rely on you on trying to get the Registrar to explain to the next witness that this is not being done capriciously.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll speak to the witness myself. I informed him yesterday that his testimony may be delayed for about an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's important that someone does explain to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Brdjanin is here. Incidentally, Mr. Ackerman -- let's proceed. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want to talk to you now about cause of death, and I begin on your Stakic report, S 281-E page 11, you say in that report, describing the killings that were committed in the municipality of Prijedor: "As a general rule, as a general result" - I'm sorry - "As a general result, it appears that the majority of victims exhumed was of non-Serb ethnicity and did not die as a result of combat activity." Please tell the Chamber the criteria you used to determine whether or not a person died of combat activity.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evidence and the information allowed us, allowed me to determine whether a person had died as a result of combat activity or not. This evidence was testimony from witnesses, from family members, the declarations, the declarations of death, concerning persons who were still recorded as missing at the time of the declaration. This is the evidence used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it had nothing to do with the kinds of injuries that appeared on the bodies that were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The types of injuries discovered on the bodies are important in that they can corroborate parts of information provided by witnesses or by family members who can talk about the time when the person was killed. In certain cases witnesses mentioned people who had been detained in certain camps, they mentioned the fact that people had been beaten, they described beatings, there were autopsy reports established by forensic scientists that indicated whether there were any fractures to the ribs or to the upper or lower body parts. When someone talks about a person who was executed, it is obvious that part of the work consists of verifying whether this is corroborated by the forensic report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically why you -- it's a sort of a jigsaw puzzle that you try to build up or bring -- put together, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in that all of these elements, if you take them individually, they provide indications but not an explanation. When you take all these elements together, view them as a whole, this allows one to corroborate one hypothesis rather than another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if we take an example, I don't recollect now the details of your report, but if you were given an indication that in a particular site you should be able to find the bodies, the remains, of X, Y and Z, and you are further given an indication that X, Y and Z were killed or died, were charred to death, were burnt to death, I would take it that you would expect in the exhumation to find some indication that those remains were -- are the remains or were the remains of someone who was burnt to death or who was burnt, anyway; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If the forensic examination allows one to find such elements. In this case, I would use a particular example. An exhumation site which concerns -- which is in the municipality of Kljuc, it concerns the village of Kurevo. Three exhumation sites were related to the incident in the village of Kurevo, in the municipality of Kljuc. One of the witnesses described that when he was taken from Kurevo some of the people from the village were killed and then on the road to Peci the convoy stopped, another part of the people were killed in a field, and then the survivors ended up in the village of Peci where they all had their hands tied with wire and were beaten. One of the individuals, who survived this walk, to Peci died in the course of the night. The body was taken to the place where he was found a few years later he was exhumed and these -- this wire with which his hands had been attached and which had been described by the witness was found. Such elements are taken into consideration in order to corroborate the version of a given witness with regard to a certain incident. This is one of many examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I said, it's a jigsaw puzzle which you bring together various pieces which could be material facts resulting from the exhumation as well as information and details for which you have to rely on others, because you -- I take it that you did not or you were not involved in the investigation of any of these crimes or any of these killings, if there were killings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this particular case, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, he's back in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, some of these bodies that were exhumed, as you've just told us, showed -- exhibited injuries that you described as resulting from blunt trauma; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In certain cases, the forensic report indicated that there were such injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you would agree that in a body found in a grave like that, that that blunt trauma -- it's virtually impossible to tell whether it's pre-mortem or post-mortem, whether it occurred before death or after death, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you don't think that you are qualified enough to answer that question, then ask me to excuse you from answering it. Because this is a technical matter. It falls within forensic pathology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer requires a forensic knowledge. With regard to a large number of autopsies I could be mistaken. For instance, a forensic scientist might make a distinction between injuries that seemed to be pre-mortem or post-mortem to him. In cases when he can't determine that there was an injury that occurred before death, then he will say that the cause of death wasn't determined. Naturally this is the role of the forensic scientist to determine such matters. It's his role rather than mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually, sir, I'm referring to something you said in your Stakic report, S281-E at page 33. On that page you're talking about the Hrastova Glavica exhumation. And what you told us in that report, "In addition to the fatal injuries, a number of bodies showed evidence of blunt trauma injuries. The examining pathologists were unable to determine whether these injuries were ante-mortem or post-mortem, before death or after death," and that was certainly the case with regard -- you understood that was the case with regard to Hrastova Glavica?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, as far as determining the cause of death is concerned, one relies on the autopsy reports established by the forensic pathologist. When it's possible to determine the cause of death, precisely, this is indicated in the report and when this isn't possible, this is also indicated. A body does not always have just one injury. A body can have several injuries, a gunshot wound, wound caused by blunt object as well as fractures in which cases the forensic pathologist can't determine the cause. In that case, you can say that you can have a body with gunshot wounds to the head or fractures to the upper or lower parts of the body and the forensic pathologist will perhaps not be able to determine whether these injuries were inflicted before or after death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, for instance, a couple of incidents come to my mind just sitting here, the -- I'm sure you're familiar with the events that occurred on Mount Vlasic when some people were shot and went over the edge of a deep ravine or I know you're familiar with a -- we talked about it earlier today, the mine shaft in which the World War Two bodies were found or bodies were dumped into a mine shaft. One would expect, I take it, in both of those instances if you were to recover those bodies, that you would probably find evidence of blunt trauma that occurred from the post-mortem or probably post-mortem injuries resulting from falling over a cliff or down the mine shaft. That makes sense, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Only answer the question if you think you're qualified to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only rely on the examination conducted by the forensic pathologist. The examination conducted of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll leave that alone now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your progress report of 13 August, 2001, Exhibit P2007, you're talking about what you describe as your proof of death projects. And in the first paragraph, this sentence appears, "All the individuals for whom proof of their death was received, are non-Serbs." You see that?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what I'm wondering is, is why you only received proof of death information regarding non-Serbs. What happened to the proof of death information regarding Serbs? Why didn't you receive that? Did you not ask for it? Or what?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as proof of death is concerned, I would just like to remind you that it's to be distinguished from the exhumations. Proof of death concerned persons who had been declared dead by municipal courts and who at the time, when they were declared dead, were still considered to be missing persons. What I also point out in my report is that these rulings declaring missing people as people who were dead, come from two municipal courts, the municipal court of Sanski Most and the Kljuc court. These courts receive people who used to live in Prijedor, Kotor Varos and Bosanski Novi and they received declarations from family members, requests asking them to declare their family members who were missing as being dead. As far as these elements are concerned, these rulings declaring that people were dead, I only received declarations that concerned persons who were non-Serbs, persons who weren't Serbs, from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that part I knew and I was I probably should have been a little more clear in my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so too because that's the answer I expected from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The concern that I have, the question that I have is this: Aren't there such court judgements from courts in Republika Srpska, for instance, dealing with declarations of death for Serbs who disappeared during the war? And if there aren't, I don't know why, and if there are, why don't you have them and why don't you report them to us? That's what I'm really trying to find out.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question. I would just like to refer you to the investigations I conducted to obtain information on exhumations of Serb victims. For the moment I've only been able to obtain general figures but I haven't been able to receive specific detailed documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to get to that a little later so let's save that for a little later. The answer is you don't have any of that kind of information?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. If you turn just a couple of pages, to the ERN number 0502, there is a table regarding these death declarations, these proof of death project death declarations for the year 1992, these being declarations from courts. You'll notice in the table that's called figure 03 that for Banja Luka, we see eight people; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And for Celinac, we see zero?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Celinac isn't mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The vast majority of the numbers in that particular table actually are from Prijedor, aren't they? It's over a thousand.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the only other municipality that's even close is Sanski Most with 226; right?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the second municipality in terms of the number of declarations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any idea with regard to these court declarations of death what the standard of proof is that's required by the judges before they make a declaration that someone is dead? Do you have any idea? And if not, that's okay. You can just say you don't.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar in detail with the law that allows an individual to request that a court, a municipal court, in ex-Yugoslavia, declare that one of their family members is deceased. I can try to summarise this procedure on the basis of my memory but it's not really my field. If a family asks for one of its family members to be declared dead, the date when the person went missing is taken into consideration. It seems that there is a time period that is required to show that the person has not appeared since disappearing, and then basing itself on these indications provided by witnesses and family members before the Court, in such cases, the person is declared dead, a ruling is issued and after a certain period of time, which I am not sure of, if this person has not yet appeared, the person is declared dead. Very briefly, if I'm not mistaken, that is the procedure that is followed in such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we -- I want to look now at your most recent addendum, 16 May Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 17415 to 17424. of 2003. And go to page 5, we are still dealing with proof of death data base, and this gives us, I think, your latest figures, and that would show that for 1992, the proof of death data base shows 774 cases of persons who died or disappeared during the year 1992 in the ARK region, 1.774; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you reduced then this figure by deaths that resulted from combat or from natural causes and by those that have been exhumed and identified and accounted for then elsewhere. You finally come down to 1.277 declarations of death for those who died or disappeared in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in your -- back again to your first report. In that first report, that being P2007, 13 August, 2001, and the ERN number page ends with 0496, there are three commissions, I believe, that are concerned with the tracing of missing persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there are only two now, the federal commission which has a branch for the Bosniak Muslims and a branch for the Bosnian Croats and a commission from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the time you wrote this first report, there was the Bosnian state commission, the RS commission, and the Croat branch of -- I think you called it the Croat branch of the federal commission, and what you said about those commissions was that basically they were each concerned with and in charge of exhuming individuals of their own ethnicity. So the Bosnian state commission for Muslims, the RS commission for Serbs and the Croat branch for Croats. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In generally speaking, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the Republika Srpska commission on tracing missing and detained persons, I think the figure at the present time that you're aware of is that they have exhumed 1.793 bodies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These exhumations which were conducted throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from 1996 to 2000. It's not just the Autonomous Region of Krajina so it's necessary to bear in mind that these are general figures, not just figures, for the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. And the other part of that is that you're presumption based upon what we just talked about, was that these 1.793 bodies exhumed are bodies of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you have not gathered together, and I'd like to know why, the kind of detailed information regarding these deaths that you have gathered together from the Bosnian authorities, have you?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't -- we didn't request to have declarations of death concerning people who died in the region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you have learned, you've been told by a member of that RS commission, I think it was, that of the 1.793 exhumations done by RS, that 1.076 of those have been identified as military personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is information that I obtained on the basis of the publication of an article that had to do with a report of a group of experts that the three commissions had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And have you made any inquiry, or do you know, the basis upon which that RS commission concluded that 1.076 of these individuals were military personnel?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have a look at two paragraphs lower down in the report, you'll see that in fact I required all -- I requested all the information that concerned the exhumations conducted by the Republika Srpska commission in the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and I didn't only ask for the date when the person died and the circumstances under which the person died and all the documents, I asked for all the documents that I asked with regard to other exhumations and I still have not received a response to this day. And that is why the figures are mentioned but unfortunately, I was not able to go into all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And because you don't have any detail regarding these matters, this information was basically excluded from your data bases, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no information concerning the places of exhumation, the exhumation dates, the information concerning the bodies, whether they were men, women or anything else. I have not received anything. I only have a general figures, and therefore, there was nothing to put into the data base.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look now at -- it's the same report, the ERN number, page is 0495 and you have a table of the figures from the Bosnian state commission for tracing missing persons. And this table apparently has to do with exhumations done by the Bosnian authorities under guidance of the Bosnian state commission and lists the number of sites and the number of individuals for several municipalities. Do you see the table I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have that copy. Are you talking about paragraph 2.3?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You have it? All right. If you look at Banja Luka, it says that from two sites, five individuals were recovered; correct?
