utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look at Celinac, it says from one site, three individuals were recovered?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's out of a total of 1.781; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Big numbers of course are Prijedor, 535; Kljuc, 463; Sanski Most, 430; right?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, once again, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now we are going to go to your most recent report, and that's P2008 and I want to go to page 6. And this would give us the most recent numbers and I'm now referring to numbers from the exhumation data base. Numbers relevant to the indictment in this case. You tell us at the very top of page 6, 419 graves, 1.872 bodies.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, of these 1.872, if we look at the table on page 9, the vast majority of those 1.872 are male, by my calculations, 91.2 per cent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a table somewhere, Mr. Ackerman, that specifies precisely how many were male, how many were female.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 9, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The vast majority were persons of military age, by my calculation 81.7 per cent.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 2.200 [As interpreted] persons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sebire, the interpreter could not hear you. I may ask to you come nearer to the microphone and could I ask to you repeat your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, I'm sorry. I am saying that there were 1261 persons aged 17 to 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1261? Is that the correct figure that you're giving us, 1.261?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, individuals aged 17 to 60, that is indeed the figure that I gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Does that satisfy you, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think Mr. Sebire would agree with me that that figure may be increased by as much as 28 because there were 28 people who it was impossible to tell they ranged anywhere from 20 to 80 or 25 to 80 years old so that 1261 figure could actually be enhanced by 28 if we knew the answer to those other 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you take into account then, yes, the number of persons in addition to those, then, yes, that would be, yes, you could indeed increase that figure, you're quite right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you now turn the page, I think it's either a different table or the same one continued, it talks about injuries. The vast majority of cause of death of these people was gunshot wounds or explosive devices, by my calculation that accounts for 92.7 per cent of the deaths.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed. The vast majority of bodies had gunshot wounds, 1.341, in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you have to add another 23 that died of explosive devices, according to this, and I suggest to you if you do that, you find that 92.7 per cent of the deaths resulted from gunshot wounds or explosive devices.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can merely take you for your word that that is the correct percentage. I do not have one myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, these are the kind of wounds, gunshot wounds and wounds from explosive devices, these are the kind of wounds you would expect to result from military combat, aren't they? That's how people die in combat, gunshot wounds and explosive devices; right?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, but in our particular instance, let me remind you once again that the majority of the bodies that were exhumed did indeed show such injuries and in the majority case in 1.305 cases we found those that indicated -- therefore it was concluded that they were not the result of the combat. That is you do not -- you can see the cause of death, that is what you can establish but you cannot say how that particular wound was inflicted. The explosive device, the deaths caused by explosive devices need not be the result of combat only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This part of the transcript, Mr. Ackerman, and Ms. Sutherland or Mrs. Richterova needs a little bit of fine-tuning because particularly the first four lines are not clear enough. So will you go through it later on or perhaps we could have it cleared up now. The witness started by saying: "Generally speaking, yes, but in one particular instance let me remind you once again that the majority of the bodies that were exhumed did indeed show such injuries and the majority in 1305 cases we found those that indicated there is something missing, there are -- it was concluded that they were not the result of combat." This needs to be cleared up. And you need to specify at least for the purposes of the transcript because I know that you did say it, for the purposes of the transcript, you need to specify on what basis it was concluded that in these cases, the wounds or the gunshot wounds and wounds from explosive devices were not the result of combat activity. Because basically that's the essence of the question that Mr. Ackerman was putting to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only go back to what was already said in this courtroom. Once that the forensic pathologist established the cause of death, if the following investigation allows us to check whether that injury was caused during an execution or in the course of a combat but if I go back and give you the most practical example and I'm therefore going back to the exhumations at Redak, then -- the testimony indicates that we were dealing with an execution there and the use of automatic rifles to fire at persons who got off a bus. These persons when the autopsy was used we found four or five wounds per person. And the fact that we found gunshot wounds corresponds to what the witnesses said. The identification also showed us that they were indeed the persons who were killed on that date and at that particular location. As you mentioned, Mr. President, a moment ago, it was -- it was like a jigsaw puzzle that you mentioned before, where you have to put pieces together. If we have 100 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's enough. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to take you just very -- well, I'm going to skip this part, Your Honour, because I think we need to finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I would invite to you bring your cross-examination to an end if possible, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've just got about 2 or 3 more questions, Judge, and then I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look at your annex 1. Your annex one attached to your addendum of 16 May, 2003. And that's at ERN number ends with 7901. It's page 1 of annex 1. And the first three entries therein have to do with exhumations in the municipality of Banja Luka. You see those?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, somewhere else, let me see if I can find it real quickly, yes. You also have an annex BO 1. So in annex 1 you speak of three exhumations in Banja Luka, Culumi, Kostici, two exhumations, five bodies; Banja Luka cemetery, two exhumations -- one exhumation, two bodies, total of seven from Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, seven in total, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now if we go to annex BL 1, which is ERN number 7928, of the five bodies that were exhumed at the two Culumi, Kostici exhumations what we learn is that these were five people who were apparently killed by the Sugic brothers; correct? Certainly the Sugic brothers --

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me find the annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. It's annex BL 1 and the ERN number is 02927928.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And the indication is that these people were killed by the Sugic brothers; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go to the next page, 7929, that gives us information about the other two of the seven that were exhumed from the Banja Luka cemetery and those people actually were Esad Bender and Omer Filipovic who it's contended were killed during the time they were confined in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that would account for all seven of the Banja Luka exhumations, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go then back to annex 1, the second page of annex 1, and that would be page 2 of annex 1 or ERN number 7902, we see an entry for Celinac, the location of the exhumation being Bastasi. It indicates three bodies but it's greyed out and I don't think there is any further information in the other annexes about that exhumation and I'm not sure you've ever told us why but I want to know why. Why don't we have more information about that?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I testified on the 30th May, I said that in annex 1, all the locations which are grey were excluded from the report, either because the exhumations took place in municipalities which were not taken into consideration in our investigations or because we had not received any information that would have allowed us to relate these exhumations to our -- to the -- to our investigation. So in Celinac, as you can see, since it is grey, that means that these results, the results there were not considered in the report which was prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you have no information about how, when or anything else regarding the death of these three people in the Celinac exhumation; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I did not receive any information regarding this exhumation, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sebire, thank you very much for your patience. You've been a very patient witness. I appreciate it. And thank you for trying to deal with my questions as best you could and I'm finished with you now. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Sebire, that means that basically, unless there are some -- is there a re-examination? All right. So.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take your time, Madam Richterova. There is a re-examination. So it's only a couple of questions from Madam Richterova and then you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Sebire, on 10th of June, you were asked by the Defence about Jama Lisac exhumation site and about the people who were identified, and you mentioned among others Edna Dautovic, and Sadeta Medunjanin. And the Defence question was and the two cases were cause of death was not established, do you know if that would have been Ms. Dautovic and Ms. Medunjanin and you were unable to answer this question. I would like to submit autopsy reports and identification reports of these persons. There are four copies for the judges and one copy for the Defence, if you would be so kind. These autopsy reports were also on the CD which was disclosed to the Defence, but they haven't been exhibited. So I would like to tender these three documents into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You're tendering these in hard copies, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In hard copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. For the record I think we need to identify them. We have been given first autopsy report bearing date 28th July of the year 2000 and starting with the ERN number 01049433. This is being marked what?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This will be marked P2024.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2024. Yes. The second document is dated 27th July, 2000. It's also an autopsy report and it starts with the ERN number 01049790. And this is being tendered and admitted as P?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2025. Thank you, Madam Richterova. And the third of these documents is a report which has four numbers on the genetic identification of bodies found in Bosnia-Herzegovina, issued, I assume, by the Instituto Nacional de Toxicologia in Madrid on the 1st of September, 2000, and it has ERN number -- the first page bears ERN number 01033936. And that will be given exhibit number P2026.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show also these three documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And if we could have a look at the autopsy report for the case 42 B which we can read then later from the identification report was identified as Edna Dautovic and if you could read us on the page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll adopt the system that we adopt in my jurisdiction, Ms. Richterova. If these documents speak for themselves, we leave it at that. I mean, --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, of course I would adopt your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you that there will not be a single document that has been tendered in evidence that we will not go through thoroughly. I can assure you of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just I will really just summarise the cause of death in both cases were gunshots and it's what I want to clarify from the -- your testimony on 10th of June, 2003. The other thing which I wanted to clarify and we have had some problems with numbers and translations, and this has something to do with Kasapnica, when we were talking about the witness who claimed 18 bodies, and you put into your report 0 bodies, and in the transcript, and I will read it, it says, "As you just pointed out, there was no way to determine the number of victims, and that's why we put in the number 18." Was it what you stated at that date? Did you really add 18 bodies or 0 bodies?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say that I'm almost sure that we considered the figure of zero and we did not consider the figure of 18, but the figure of zero in so far as Kasapnica is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So to be absolutely sure, these 18 bodies mentioned by the witness were excluded from your report?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SEBIRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That's all what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in cutting off a series of questions, I also cut off an exhibit which I intended to present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I'd like permission to do that. It doesn't require any testimony from the witness but I intended to present it during his testimony and so let me hand this to the usher, for distribution. Please give one to the Prosecutor and I've got one for each of the Judges and the rest for... It's marked DB141A. And it's an article from the June 11th, 2003, edition of the International Herald Tribune, Your Honour and I would ask that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I can't see the relevance of this document for our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps before admitting it, Mr. Ackerman, because just even for purposes of the publicity of the hearing itself, this speaks about Iraq, toll of civilians put at 3.240 and it's extracted from the International Herald Tribune of June 11, 2003. What do you intend to prove by means or to show by means of this newspaper report?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it gives us perspective. We are talking here about an almost a year's worth of activity in the ARK area of Bosnia-Herzegovina as compared with one month of war in Iraq, and the number of civilians killed in Iraq is dramatically greater than what appears to have been killed in this war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think it gives us perspective, especially with regard to the allegations of genocide or crimes against humanity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it will be admitted for that purpose only, and I do notice that sometimes you too rely or choose to rely on newspaper reports, Mr. Ackerman, and bring them forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As Mr. Cunningham would say, it comes from the famous case of goose versus gander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The witness can now leave. Mr. Sebire, may I express the Chamber's gratitude and appreciation for your patience which was also pointed out by Mr. Ackerman? Thank you. And you may now leave the courtroom. Mr. Ackerman, may I also take the opportunity to thank you publicly for the exemplary cross-examination, which I wish could be made available to students, because it's an education.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that. I would like to be excused so I can go not to rest but today to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you can rest on your own laurels now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to go work, Your Honour, thank you very much and I'll take my laurels with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be excused as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I excuse you as well, Madam Richterova, let's organise our schedule for today and tomorrow. Now, we have got two witnesses. One is BT56, which is the next one and then we also have BT55. Do I take it that you are handling BT55? Who is handling 55?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is the witness for tomorrow, yes, I'm handling that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And who will be taking BT55 tomorrow for cross-examination, you Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also BT56?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So more or less and I know this is not exactly a question that can get a clear, straightforward answer, but more or less basing yourself on what you have read in the statements of these two persons, how long do you anticipate your cross-examination to last in both cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: With respect to the witness today, I don't anticipate it will be very long at all simply because of the subject matter. I anticipate maybe 15, 20 minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right and the other one?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Tomorrow it will be a little bit longer. When I've talked to the Prosecution, they indicated to me, maybe about a hour's worth of testimony on their presentation in chief. I would think approximately that much on cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another hour, an hour on this. So you think you will require what, one hour for the direct, Madam Richterova with BT55?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I again want to take your advice and I am going to submit his previous statement, tender his previous statement into evidence and really go very briefly through his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm trying to cover Ms. Sutherland as much as I can so as not to make her life difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When I said one hour, it's really maximum one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we take it we require roughly two clear hours tomorrow for BT55, which leaves us with an hour and a half roughly tomorrow, an hour and a half, or an hour and a quarter, plus we have half an hour plus another hour and another three-quarters of an hour. So more or less out of the one hour and a quarter that we have today, and a hour and a half that you will -- or another hour and a quarter that you have tomorrow minus the 15 minutes or 20 minutes, make it 30 minutes that Mr. Cunningham will require, you need to finish your direct in -- that means two hours and a half -- in two hours. So adjust yourself accordingly. I have gone through the witness's statements, both of them, and unless we really -- you really have information that you will require from the witness, that goes beyond what is stated in the statement, or unless you need to clarify what is stated in the statements, and there is one point I will come to straight away, I would ask you to refer to the statement as much as you can and try to limit your direct to that as much as you can. Because otherwise, I know that if you go beyond that, you will not make it in two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been instructed to take the witness through the statement and not lead him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So then there is one point that I want to point out to you before he comes in straight away, something that I have noticed. When he speaks of Lieutenant Colonel Zijad Selimovic, he speaks about this person in both statements. In the latter of the two statements on page 3, and he says, "We carried his body to the gymnasium in Petar Kocic school and on the following day we buried him," and he also speaks about him on several parts of the previous statement. On page 5, he says that, "Selimovic was shot and killed after he was ordered to go sit in the anti-aircraft gunner and then a Serb from the unit shot him." And then there is: "I did not see this happen but Selimovic son-in-law did. He later disappeared." I want to know who disappeared, whether it's the son-in-law that disappeared, because it's not clear, or whether it's a contradiction with what he said in his previous statement, that is that they carried his body and buried him. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's one part I definitely want to you clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be doing my best to go through his testimony as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just on your mathematics I thought we had three hours for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My mathematics are not --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: An hour and a quarter today, an hour and a quarter tomorrow which is 3 and a half hours, Mr. Cunningham requires 15, 20 minutes -- which would leave me three hours in chief, not two hours; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: More or less. But anyway, I told you my mathematics are not -- have never been impressive. And they still aren't, not like yours, Mr. Brdjanin, I suppose, being an engineer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will need the blinds down before the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But initially only, he's not in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. Pseudonym and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So while we bring the witness in, we will have the blinds down. So thank you, Mr. Ackerman, we will see you tomorrow, I suppose, unless -- and incidentally, Simic case, they had two weeks for the Rule 98 and the last case, again two weeks, so that seems to be a real maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It went for over -- yeah, but anyway, we will talk about that later. So, usher, you can bring the witness in, please. So this one, bring me -- update me, please, Ms. Sutherland, he's got a pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And image, not voice distortion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And I'll explain the protective measures myself to him. Don't bother about them yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you raise the sound level, usher, please? Good morning to you, sir. I see you with a smiling face now so I take it you have finally succeeded in having interpretation of what I am saying in a language that you can understand. So I welcome you to this Tribunal and to this case that we are handling. You will soon be giving testimony and our rules require that before you do so, you enter a solemn declaration, stating that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained in a piece of paper that is being handed out to you. Please read that text aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a chair. I suppose the usher can pull the curtains up, draw the curtains up again. And sir, I will try and explain to you the basics of what's going to happen. First of all, I am pleased to inform you that the protective measures that you asked from us, that is that you will not be referred to by your name and that no one would be able to see an image of yourself, of your face, we have granted. We have agreed to grant you these protective measures. The idea being in order to hide and protect your identity for reasons that were made clear to us by the Prosecution and which were also accepted by the Defence. That's number 1. So basically, if -- usher help him, please, and may I ask the cameras to focus on the witness? And put his video monitor on video screen, on video? Well, that's how others will be seeing you. In other words, no one should be able to identify your face behind those cubes. That's what we call a distorted image of yourself. You are also going to be referred to by a number, and that's BT56. No one will refer to you by your name here, in order again to protect your identity, but you must also help us. There will be moments when you will be asked certain questions which will require us or require from you to give us certain details and for those we will go into private session. And that means that no one will be able to hear what you will be telling us outside of this courtroom. But when we are not in private session, you ought to be careful yourself not to mention your name, your family name or the names of your family members or other facts or indications that could reveal your identity. You understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You will first be asked a series of questions by Ms. Sutherland, who I'm sure you've met already, and she will then be followed by Mr. Cunningham for Radoslav Brdjanin, who is the accused in this case. We won't finish today. We will finish with you tomorrow. And before you start giving evidence, may I on behalf of the Trial Chamber offer you our apologise for having kept you weighing for so long before you could start your testimony. This was not done through the fault of anyone or capriciously. It's just that we couldn't finish with the other work that was scheduled before. So I'm sorry for that and I hope we have your understanding. Ms. Sutherland, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look at this piece of paper which will be handed to you by the usher. Can you please confirm by saying yes or no whether that is your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Usher, if you could show that to the Defence and then the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session for a few background details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go -- it's exhibited under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as P2027.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, please remember that we are now in open session. I want to turn now to the attack on Bosanska Krupa town. Do you recall when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes. On the 22nd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall what day of the week it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes. It was on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you told that the town would be attacked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: No. We found out about it half a day earlier perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did you find out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Well, there were rumours, citizens spoke about it, they said that there would be shooting this evening, and it happened around 6.00 p.m. So that's how we heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The people that told you this, were they of Serb or Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In the area where you lived, were the Serb population still in their houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: No. That's why I felt it. They were leaving the town on the whole. Some snipers remained in the houses with light machine guns.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How was the town attacked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: They simply started shooting at about 6.00 in the evening, both sides started shooting. I don't remember who first opened fire. It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was there any shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you during the attack? Without naming the place where you were, the person's place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless you prefer to go to private session Ms. Sutherland for the purposes of this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in my house, that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you able to see from which direction the attack was coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: From the direction of Vranjska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of the people that live in the village of Vranjska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you stay in your house that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: No. I went into another house which was 50 metres away. I went to see what the situation was like, to find out what they knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Well, it continued on the following day. The attacks continued. And in the course of that day, I was arrested in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you arrested by yourself or with other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: There were another three civilians, citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: To Jasenica, about 18 kilometres from Bosanska Krupa, to the so-called Serbian municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where in Jasenica were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: To the Jasenica school. That's where we were taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many other people were at the school when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: When I got there, there were perhaps between 10 and 11 people but as time passed, more and more people kept arriving.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were there in total?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when they occupied the town, there were about 65, 60 of us detainees who remained but there were also civilians who were sent to the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you taken from the school for questioning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them, but those who stayed in that camp or whatever it was had to go through that court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say that court, where was this building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: The building was in Jasenica, not far from the school. It was the building of the museum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will break for 25 minutes here, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brdjanin. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, may I just make a quick apology to you in relation to your mathematics. For some reason I was thinking that one and a quarter hours and two and a quarter hours gives me three and a half, but you were right, it's two hours. So I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems -- still I confirm that mathematics is not my forte, or my arithmetic. It's not mathematics because algebra and geometry

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, again I would just like to remind that you we are in open session, just before we broke I asked you a question in relation to the Court that you said that you were taken to which was in a museum building not far from the school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what else was housed in the museum building at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: No. I don't know that there was anything except that individual who was there, I mean those judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was there a military command unit headquarters in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And whereabouts was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: It was in a different building. I think that there was a small motel nearby.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So getting back to this court where you were taken for questioning, who conducted these court sessions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Those were Mladen Drljaca as the Presiding Judge, Mitar Ciganovic and Mirko Orelj was there and there was a woman there who was a recording clerk.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Taking these three individuals, first Mladen Drljaca, who was his position before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: For a while he was the secretary of the municipality. Then he was misdemeanour authority and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mitar Ciganovic, is that the person you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And his occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: He worked for a company called Brazda. It had a butcher's shop so he worked as a butcher in one of those shops.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: A Serb too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Third person, Mirko Orelj, what was his occupation before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: He also worked for Brazda, for Brazda cooperative and I think he was either an accountant. At any rate, he worked for the accountancy department there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Serb too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was anybody else present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: From time to time, Pop Ilija and Dr. Stanko Obradovic would come in now and then to kind of supervise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned a person called Pop Ilija. What was that person's occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: He was a priest, so he was Priest Ilija. I don't know. They just came in and watched and listened but he was there. He did come in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Stanko Obradovic, was he a medical doctor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes. He was a physician, and they had a small health centre there or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What sort of questions were you asked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Well, questions. Well, depends, what I knew about the war, and allegedly who was an extremist and whether we knew that fire would be opened, why hadn't we fled our houses and gone to the other bank and such like.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did the questioning last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Depends. I'd say half an hour, 20 minutes, half hour, sometimes longer. I'm not quite sure how long did it last for others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you ever told why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: He didn't tell me. I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: During the questioning by this so-called court, were you ever formally charged with any crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: I personally was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After your questioning, did you return to the Jasenica school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes. They took me back to the school to question about ten people and as soon as they would be questioned they would be sent on to Krupa to the Petar Kocic elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Jasenica school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: From the 23rd of April, until the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where within the school complex were you detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: We were in class rooms, in the school. We were in different classrooms. But in the beginning, we were in its gym and later on, they took us to the classrooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that there were between 50 and 60 people detained there. What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: They were Muslims and perhaps a few, a couple, I know of two Croats who were detained there but those Croats, one stayed on in the camp and I think that the other one was sent to Sanski Most, the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was there anyone of Serb ethnicity detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: No, not at that time. But later on, there were Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2113.7, which is a photograph? That has the ERN number 0326-5867.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you take the pointer that's on the table and point on the machine to your right, first of all, what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: It's the school in Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Using the pointer, can you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: I think, I think it's the school.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you point to where the gymnasium is located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you place the pointer and just hold it there, put the pointer on to the actual machine?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He needs to point to the photo on the ELMO, usher, please, not on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he is pointing to the one on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you look at the photograph on the machine beside you and place the pointer on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For the record you're pointing to the building which is running perpendicular to the building we can see in the foreground of the photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have another copy of that photograph. Would you like the witness to mark the photograph or is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I think we can -- that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I've finished with that photograph. Your Honour can we go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we don't need to have this put under seal now, no? Because the way you conducted the questions, I think we have avoided having to put this document under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was hoping that is the case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is the case but I want you to agree do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, we are back in open session. How were you being guarded at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Allegedly in the school where I was, there were some guards. One was -- of them was semi-civilian -- I mean, how shall I say it? He had an old rifle and the rest I don't know, and there were policemen at the entrance into the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, did you recognise any of the guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: I only knew Jojo and he was semi-civilian. He had this military shirt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the conditions you were kept in? Were you provided food and water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: We were getting tin food.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sutherland, please, could you help me? He needs to -- witness, you need to speak out a little bit louder. The interpreters are finding it a little bit difficult, and I can quite understand, because I myself can't hear what you are saying in your own language in any case. So if you come closer, please, to the microphones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps if the other microphone could be switched on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, as well. Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. And he needs to repeat what he said because the interpreter missed it. You were asked --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to do that. I was going to repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you were provided with tin food. Was there anything else that you were provided with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: No. We had those tins.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many meals a day were you given?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you have bedding to sleep on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: No. In Jasenica we slept on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you able to wash daily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: No. Not in Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were there any female detainees in Jasenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: There were two women in Jasenica, Semsa Sepic and another one. Now, her name escapes me right now, but I knew her. No, just can't remember her name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After the initial questioning, were you ever interrogated again while you were detained in the Jasenica school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Well, two, two, three times while we were in Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When was the first time, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: It was the very next day after I was arrested in the gymnasium in Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were you mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: There were a few of us in the gymnasium and the so-called Suha Rebra, "Spare Ribs" came, a few of them, and the woman, and they started pricking us with their knives on our legs, beat us with handcuffs on the head, stamping on us, so that some of us fainted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know these people were from the Suha --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Suha Rebra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know they were from that unit or did you subsequently learn that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: We found out about that later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were pricked with their knives and beaten with handcuffs on the head. What other implements or weapons did this group of people have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: They had automatic weapons, they had various knives, and I don't know, they had various -- they had quite a few bombs, I don't know how they were able to carry them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say bombs, do you mean hand grenades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What if anything did they say when they first entered into the gymnasium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Well, they said something but I can't remember what exactly. They said something like, "Do you want a state of your own?" They said something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were any derogatory terms used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: It's difficult to know. As soon as they entered, they started doing those things, the bad things that they did, so given the situation, it's difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also told us a moment ago that they were stamping on you so that some of you fainted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What injury did you sustain from this beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: I was jabbed in the leg with a knife twice. My ribs were broken and my skull was fractured.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What area of the body were they stamping on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: The kidneys, the fingers, they kicked us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you lose consciousness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes, I lost consciousness for several minutes. I wasn't aware of anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you receive any treatment for these injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Stanko appeared later on and two nurses, and they bandaged me, they had to cut my hair a bit because of all the wounds that were there, in order to cleanse the wounds, and they put some sort of bandages, some sort of plasters over the wounds caused by knives and there was some Kurtic Becir there, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many of you were beaten on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Seriously, there were four of us who were seriously wounded but there were another three who slapped people around. One was hit with a gun, one person hit a detainee with a gun over the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Apart from this beating, are you aware of other detainees receiving the same or similar treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes. Some people were in another room, in a classroom, they didn't -- they didn't jab them with knives but they beat them too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall when were you beaten on the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Yes. A day or two later, three or four men appeared. They were wearing uniforms, Seselj's uniforms. They hit me with the rifle butt and I was covered in bruises as a result of this. They beat two or three of us. There was an old man who was there too and he was also beaten by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, perhaps he can describe what he means by Seselj's uniform. That's number 1. And secondly if he could give us the name of this elderly person, if he knows it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you heard the Judge's comment. Are you able to tell the Court who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What distinguished Seselj's uniform? How would you recognise a uniform to be a Seselj's uniform? If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they themselves claimed to be Seselj's men. That's what they declared themselves to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were they dressed? You said they were in uniform. What sort of uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: They weren't in camouflage uniforms. They had olive drab uniforms, summer uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the uniforms have insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Some did. But I couldn't see them that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you weren't able to see what was actually on the insignia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Only on one case I saw that one of them was an officer, a sergeant, a senior sergeant of some kind. He had an arm band. As for the other two who were there, I didn't notice any insignia on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did the beating last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: I think it lasted for about 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you, how long did the first beating last that occurred a few -- a couple of days before this one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by the first beating.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that some men and one woman from the Suha Rebra unit entered the school. How long did that beating last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: They did that very quickly. I can't tell you how long it lasted exactly but it took maybe five to ten minutes. It wasn't just one man there. There were nine of them and a woman. Each one of them got hold of someone and beat the person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Going back to this second beating, did you lose consciousness during this beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: No. I didn't lose consciousness during the second beating but I was badly beaten. And it was hard for me to sit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After being detained for ten days in Jasenica school, where were you then taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: As I said earlier on, once we had been questioned we were all sent to Bosanska Krupa, to the Petar Kocic school.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long were you detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: If you're referring to the Petar Kocic school, well, up until the 21st of August, from when we returned. That was in Bosanska Krupa. From the 2nd of May to the 21st of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many detainees were kept in the Petar Kocic school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: Up until the exchange, those that returned from Jasenica, 50 or 60 people. I don't know the exact figure, then there were two exchanges and only 11 of them remained, but after, up until the departure for Kamenica near Drvar, there were up to 37 of them. Of those 37, 16 were killed, one person went missing, and 20 of us went to Kamenica. We went to a camp in Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Of the detainees that were in the Petar Kocic school, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT56
utterances.text: They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that's a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Sir, we have to stop here. We will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think so that we don't need to put the curtains down again? You still have to put the curtains down? No? So usher, please put the curtains down and we will leave the room once we have made sure that they are down. All right. Good afternoon. See you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 13th day of June, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
